title: Rama is dharma with a body
hookLine: flatterers are everywhere, says an old rakshasa to his king; the person who tells you the hard truth is rare

lines: A FLYING CHARIOT ALONG THE COAST.
cards: Ravana sets out again in his flying chariot, along the coast. Valmiki slows down to paint it: shores lined with coconut palms and sandalwood, pearls drying on the beaches, hermitages of sages, and merchants' ships.
Then the chariot lands at Maricha's hermitage a second time. The old rakshasa, in bark clothes and matted hair, welcomes his king with food and water, and asks, carefully: why have you come back?

teach.b: Ravana spells out the plan. Turn yourself into a golden deer, spotted with silver, and wander near Rama's hut. Sita will want you.
Rama and Lakshmana will go after you. Then I'll take her.

teach.h: PLEASANT WORDS ARE EASY TO FIND.
teach.b: Maricha begins with a saying: people who say pleasant things are always easy to find, king. But someone who says what is unpleasant and good for you, and someone who will listen to it, those are rare.
Then he tells Ravana the truth he doesn't want. You don't know who Rama is. He wasn't sent to the forest for any crime; he went to keep his father's word.
And then a short line in Sanskrit: ramo vigrahavan dharmah.

teach.h: RAMA IS DHARMA IN BODILY FORM.
teach.b: Rama is dharma in bodily form. To steal his wife is to walk into a fire. Look at who's speaking: not a sage, not a friend, but a rakshasa, Rama's old enemy, once hurled across the sea by him.
Hold on to that line, because it's how Hindus learn dharma. Dharma is a big word: right living, duty, truth, the order that holds the world together. It's hard to learn from a definition.

So the tradition gives you a person. When a child asks what dharma looks like, many Hindu families point to Rama: keeping his father's word, faithful to Sita, protecting the sages, warning his enemies before he fights.
You don't memorize dharma. You watch it, and walk after it.

how: Maricha's line ramo vigrahavan dharmah, Rama is dharma in bodily form, is quoted on its own in Hindu teaching, as are his lines on rare, honest advice.

o: a royal law that a king writes for his people
right living, duty and truth, all in one word
the fate a person can't escape, whatever they do

games.q: the second visit — tap the pairs.
p: a golden deer with silver spots
one who speaks and hears hard truth
Rama is dharma in bodily form

s: dharma just means religion, or a list of rules
it means right living, duty and truth; Maricha points to a person, Rama, to show what it looks like.
the well-known line that Rama is dharma in bodily form is spoken by a sage
it's spoken by Maricha, a rakshasa and Rama's old enemy.
Maricha says Rama wasn't exiled for any crime
he went to keep his father's word.

games.q: you're Maricha. your king wants you to lure Rama away so he can steal Sita. what do you tell him?
o: the hard truth: Rama is dharma itself, and this will ruin you.
games.why: Maricha tells him the hard truth, plainly. tomorrow: what Ravana does with it.

practice: Bring to mind someone who told you something you didn't want to hear that turned out to be true and good for you, the rare kind Maricha talks about. Picture their face as they said it, and notice what it cost them.
Let a little gratitude rise. If you can, send them a short thank-you text after the sit.

wordCard.voice: Dharma: right living, duty, truth. Maricha tells his king that flatterers are easy to find, and that Rama is dharma in bodily form.

orig.note: Sanskrit: 'Rama is dharma with a body,' Maricha's line in Aranya 37.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: dharma has a body, and it's Rama. The rare friend says the hard thing, and the rare listener hears it. See you tomorrow.
